summary: Discusses models and design considerations for a SIP overload control mechanism. SIP servers can run out of resources and the 503 response code provides only limited protection, so overload remains a danger. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When too many callers ring at once, a switchboard gets overwhelmed. This describes why SIP phone systems need a better way to say slow down, and what to think about when designing one.

questions: how to prevent sip server overload
subtitle: Design framework for mechanisms to prevent SIP servers from becoming overloaded

tldr.problem: SIP servers can become overloaded when the number of SIP messages they receive exceeds their processing capacity. The existing 503 (Service Unavailable) response code provides only limited protection and can actually worsen the problem through retransmissions, causing congestion collapse where throughput drops dramatically.
tldr.mechanism: The document presents a framework for SIP overload control with three main approaches: hop-by-hop (each server controls the load sent by its direct neighbor), end-to-end (overload information flows from destination back to source), and local (a server rejects excess messages locally). Servers use monitoring, control functions, and feedback mechanisms to manage load.
tldr.outcome: Operators can design overload control mechanisms that keep SIP servers operating near maximum capacity during peak traffic, prevent congestion collapse, and maintain service quality by explicitly signaling when to reduce traffic instead of relying on packet loss.

facts.label: Congestion collapse outcome
facts.value: Throughput can drop to 10% of maximum capacity

today: RFC 6357 is an Informational RFC published in August 2011, providing the design framework for SIP overload control. The IETF subsequently developed RFC 7339 and RFC 8218 (SIP Overload Control) which provide specific protocol mechanisms based on these design principles. Most modern SIP servers and proxies now implement some form of overload control to prevent congestion collapse during peak traffic periods.

sections.title: The SIP Overload Problem
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is the standard signaling protocol for voice over IP (VoIP) and other real-time communications. A SIP server handles incoming SIP messages (requests and responses) to set up, manage, and tear down calls. Like any server, a SIP server has finite resources (CPU, memory, I/O, disk) and can become overloaded when the number of incoming messages exceeds its processing capacity.

The problem is worse in SIP than in many other protocols because of congestion collapse. When a SIP server over UDP is overloaded and starts dropping messages, the sending systems (clients and upstream servers) do not know their messages were dropped—they just see no response. So they retry the messages according to SIP retransmission timers. Each retry adds more load to the already overloaded server, creating a vicious cycle where throughput plummets instead of stabilizing. A SIP server at 80% capacity might only deliver 10% of its maximum throughput if overloaded due to retransmissions.
sections.plainLanguage: When a telephone switchboard gets too many calls, bad things happen. Without feedback, people keep trying again, making the problem worse. The system needs a way to tell callers to slow down before it completely breaks.

sections.title: System Model and Components
sections.content:
An overload control mechanism consists of four key components working together in a feedback loop. The SIP Processor processes SIP messages and is the component being protected. The Monitor measures the current load of the SIP Processor (for example, CPU usage, memory consumption, or message queue depth) and reports load samples to the Control Function. The Control Function receives load samples from the Monitor and determines if overload is occurring and what throttle (a rate limit or message drop percentage) should be applied. The Actuator implements the throttle by controlling how many messages are forwarded to the downstream SIP server, using techniques like message gapping or selective message rejection.

The control loop works bidirectionally: one server (receiving entity) measures its load and sends feedback (F) about the throttle it needs to its upstream neighbor (sending entity). The upstream neighbor's Actuator applies this throttle, reducing the traffic it sends. In more complex scenarios with multiple servers along a path, multiple feedback loops may operate in parallel, each controlling one hop or the entire path depending on the design.
sections.plainLanguage: A server has a doctor (Monitor) checking its health, a brain (Control Function) deciding what to do, and a gatekeeper (Actuator) letting through only as many callers as it can handle. The gatekeeper tells upstream gatekeepers to let fewer people through.

sections.title: Three Cooperation Models
sections.content:
Hop-by-Hop Overload Control creates independent control loops between each pair of neighboring SIP servers. When server B becomes overloaded, it sends feedback to its direct upstream neighbor A, telling it to reduce traffic. Server A acts on this feedback by rejecting or redirecting messages. If server A also becomes overloaded (due to other reasons), it sends feedback to its upstream neighbors, which take action independently. The advantage is simplicity: each server only manages traffic to its direct neighbors, feedback doesn't cross trust boundaries, and the mechanism scales well. The disadvantage is that feedback from downstream servers doesn't propagate all the way upstream, so an originating server may not know about distant overloads.

End-to-End Overload Control consolidates overload information from all SIP servers along the entire path of a request (from caller through all proxies to the called party) and uses this information to throttle traffic at the source. This can be more efficient because the source knows about all overloads along the path. However, it is complex: sources must track overload status of many servers, routing decisions can be unpredictable, and this approach requires multi-hop feedback across trust boundaries.

Local Overload Control is implemented within a single SIP server, where the Monitor and Actuator run on the same server. The server monitors its own resources and rejects excess messages locally to prevent overload. This provides a last-resort protection mechanism but cannot prevent congestion collapse alone, because rejecting messages still consumes resources and doesn't prevent retransmissions from worsening the problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Hop-by-hop is like asking your neighbor to slow down when you're busy, and trusting they'll ask their neighbor if they get busy. End-to-end is like sending a message all the way back to the original caller. Local is like your switchboard just dropping calls when full. Each has trade-offs.

sections.title: Feedback Mechanisms and Control Types
sections.content:
Overload control mechanisms differ in how they signal overload from the receiving entity back to the sending entity. Explicit Overload Control sends an explicit signal (feedback) from the overloaded server to its upstream neighbor, telling it to reduce traffic. This feedback can take different forms: Rate-Based feedback specifies a target rate (e.g., 'reduce traffic to 50 INVITE/sec'), Loss-Based feedback specifies a percentage to reject (e.g., 'drop 30% of messages'), Window-Based feedback (similar to TCP flow control) specifies a window size ('accept only 100 concurrent transactions'), and Signal-Based feedback uses simple on/off signals ('I'm overloaded' or 'I'm OK'). Explicit control enables a server to steer incoming load to a rate at which it can operate at maximum capacity.

Implicit Overload Control uses the absence of responses (packet loss) as the signal of overload. When an upstream server sends a message and doesn't receive a response in time, it infers that the downstream server is overloaded and reduces traffic. This is more robust because it doesn't depend on the overloaded server taking action, but it is less efficient because the upstream server only learns about overload after messages are already lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Explicit feedback is like a sign saying 'slow down 50%' or 'we're full, reject everything for now'. Implicit feedback is like a caller not getting an answer and deciding not to try again for a while.

sections.title: Topologies, Fairness, and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Different SIP network topologies create different challenges for overload control. In a load balancer configuration, one server distributes traffic to multiple downstream servers; the load balancer can intelligently direct new traffic to servers with capacity. In a multiple sources configuration, one server receives traffic from multiple upstream neighbors and must fairly allocate its limited capacity among them. A mesh topology combines both scenarios. An edge proxy receives traffic from thousands of diverse clients, each sending only a few messages; traditional rate-limiting is ineffective here.

When an overloaded server must reduce traffic from multiple upstream neighbors, it must decide on a fairness policy. Basic fairness gives each request equal probability of success. Customized fairness allocates resources according to service level agreements (SLAs) or other priorities, allowing different upstream neighbors to receive different levels of service.

Performance metrics for an overload control mechanism include goodput (the throughput delivered under overload—ideally a server should maintain its maximum capacity even under heavy load), delay (overload control should not significantly increase message delays, which would cause timeouts and retransmissions), and stability (the mechanism should quickly dampen oscillations in traffic and prevent repeated cycles of overload).
sections.plainLanguage: Different network shapes need different strategies. A switchboard serving thousands of one-time callers can't tell them all to reduce their rate. Instead it drops a percentage of incoming calls. Some customers might pay for priority. Success is measured by how much work gets done, how long calls take to connect, and whether things stay stable.
